title: Impact of Road Density on Urban Population Growth

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Instrumental Variables (2SLS)
- Rationale: Road density (x) is potentially endogenous in the population growth equation (y) because urban areas expecting faster growth may lobby for, or attract, more roads (reverse causality), and there may be omitted determinants of both roads and growth (e.g., geography, planning priorities). The 1947 highway plan (z) provides plausibly exogenous variation in modern road density: historical planned routes generated quasi-geographic assignment of highway access, unrelated to modern growth shocks except through roads.
- Key assumptions:
  - Relevance: z is strongly correlated with x after conditioning on controls (first-stage F-stat >> 10).
  - Exclusion: Conditional on controls (e.g., baseline income, education), the 1947 plan affects y only through its impact on road density, not via other direct channels.
  - Independence: z is as good as random with respect to unobserved determinants of y, conditional on controls.
  - Monotonicity: The plan weakly increases road density for all areas (no defiers).
  - SUTVA/No spillovers: One area’s plan-induced roads do not directly change another area’s population growth in a way that invalidates the exclusion restriction.

The IV estimate identifies the LATE: the causal effect of road density on population growth for urban areas whose road density is shifted by the 1947 plan.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Complete, self-contained R code that:
# - Reads the CSV file from the path provided
# - Runs the appropriate causal analysis
# - Prints a clear numerical result (coefficient, CAR, etc.)
# - Includes basic robustness checks

# Packages
req_pkgs <- c("AER", "sandwich", "lmtest", "car", "dplyr")
for (p in req_pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(p, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
  }
}
library(AER)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)
library(car)
library(dplyr)

# 1) Load data
path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s77_data.csv"
df <- read.csv(path)
# Basic cleaning
df <- df %>%
  select(y, x, z, controls) %>%
  mutate(z = as.numeric(z)) %>%
  na.omit()

cat("Sample size (after NA removal):", nrow(df), "\n")

# 2) Baseline OLS (naive)
ols <- lm(y ~ x + controls, data = df)
ols_vcov <- vcovHC(ols, type = "HC1")
ols_ct <- coeftest(ols, vcov = ols_vcov)
b_ols <- coef(ols)["x"]
se_ols <- sqrt(diag(ols_vcov))["x"]
p_ols <- ols_ct["x","Pr(>|t|)"]
cat("\nNaive OLS (HC1 robust):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", b_ols, se_ols, p_ols))

# 3) First-stage and Reduced-form
fs  <- lm(x ~ z + controls, data = df)
fs_vcov <- vcovHC(fs, type = "HC1")
fs_ct <- coeftest(fs, vcov = fs_vcov)
b_fs_z <- coef(fs)["z"]
se_fs_z <- sqrt(diag(fs_vcov))["z"]
p_fs_z <- fs_ct["z","Pr(>|t|)"]

rf  <- lm(y ~ z + controls, data = df)
rf_vcov <- vcovHC(rf, type = "HC1")
rf_ct <- coeftest(rf, vcov = rf_vcov)
b_rf_z <- coef(rf)["z"]
se_rf_z <- sqrt(diag(rf_vcov))["z"]
p_rf_z <- rf_ct["z","Pr(>|t|)"]

# Robust first-stage F for excluded instrument z
fs_F <- tryCatch({
  lh <- car::linearHypothesis(fs, "z = 0", vcov = fs_vcov, test = "F")
  as.numeric(lh[2,"F"])
}, error = function(e) NA)

cat("\nFirst-stage (x ~ z + controls), HC1 robust:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Coef on z = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", b_fs_z, se_fs_z, p_fs_z))
cat(sprintf("  Robust first-stage F-stat on z: %.3f\n", fs_F))

cat("\nReduced-form (y ~ z + controls), HC1 robust:\n")
cat(sprintf("  Coef on z = %.4f, SE = %.4f, p = %.4f\n", b_rf_z, se_rf_z, p_rf_z))

# 4) IV (2SLS)
iv <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls | controls + z, data = df)
iv_vcov <- vcovHC(iv, type = "HC1")
iv_ct <- coeftest(iv, vcov = iv_vcov)
b_iv <- coef(iv)["x"]
se_iv <- sqrt(diag(iv_vcov))["x"]
p_iv <- iv_ct["x","Pr(>|t|)"]
ci_low <- b_iv - 1.96 * se_iv
ci_high <- b_iv + 1.96 * se_iv

# Also report diagnostics from AER (includes weak IV and Wu-Hausman under homoskedasticity)
iv_sum_diag <- tryCatch(summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE), error = function(e) NULL)

cat("\nIV (2SLS) results, HC1 robust:\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, SE = %.4f, 95%% CI = [%.4f, %.4f], p = %.4f\n",
            b_iv, se_iv, ci_low, ci_high, p_iv))

if (!is.null(iv_sum_diag) && !is.null(iv_sum_diag$diagnostics)) {
  cat("\nAER diagnostics (classical SEs):\n")
  print(iv_sum_diag$diagnostics)
}

# 5) Wald check: reduced form / first stage
wald_iv <- b_rf_z / b_fs_z
cat("\nWald ratio (RF_z / FS_z):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x (Wald) = %.4f\n", wald_iv))

# 6) Robustness checks

# 6a) Add nonlinear control term
df <- df %>% mutate(controls_sq = controls^2)
iv_nl <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls + controls_sq | controls + controls_sq + z, data = df)
iv_nl_vcov <- vcovHC(iv_nl, type = "HC1")
b_iv_nl <- coef(iv_nl)["x"]
se_iv_nl <- sqrt(diag(iv_nl_vcov))["x"]
ci_low_nl <- b_iv_nl - 1.96 * se_iv_nl
ci_high_nl <- b_iv_nl + 1.96 * se_iv_nl
cat("\nRobustness: Add nonlinear controls (controls^2):\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, SE = %.4f, 95%% CI = [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            b_iv_nl, se_iv_nl, ci_low_nl, ci_high_nl))

# 6b) Trim outliers in x (1st-99th percentiles)
p_lo <- quantile(df$x, 0.01, na.rm = TRUE)
p_hi <- quantile(df$x, 0.99, na.rm = TRUE)
df_trim <- df %>% filter(x >= p_lo, x <= p_hi)
iv_trim <- ivreg(y ~ x + controls + controls_sq | controls + controls_sq + z, data = df_trim)
iv_trim_vcov <- vcovHC(iv_trim, type = "HC1")
b_iv_trim <- coef(iv_trim)["x"]
se_iv_trim <- sqrt(diag(iv_trim_vcov))["x"]
ci_low_trim <- b_iv_trim - 1.96 * se_iv_trim
ci_high_trim <- b_iv_trim + 1.96 * se_iv_trim

# First-stage F in trimmed sample
fs_trim <- lm(x ~ z + controls + controls_sq, data = df_trim)
fs_trim_F <- tryCatch({
  lh <- car::linearHypothesis(fs_trim, "z = 0", vcov = vcovHC(fs_trim, type = "HC1"), test = "F")
  as.numeric(lh[2,"F"])
}, error = function(e) NA)

cat("\nRobustness: Trim x to 1st–99th pct, include controls^2:\n")
cat(sprintf("  beta_x = %.4f, SE = %.4f, 95%% CI = [%.4f, %.4f]\n",
            b_iv_trim, se_iv_trim, ci_low_trim, ci_high_trim))
cat(sprintf("  Trimmed-sample robust first-stage F on z: %.3f\n", fs_trim_F))

# 7) Final concise result summary
cat("\nSummary (key estimates):\n")
cat(sprintf("  OLS beta_x (HC1)   = %.4f\n", b_ols))
cat(sprintf("  2SLS beta_x (HC1)  = %.4f (95%% CI [%.4f, %.4f])\n", b_iv, ci_low, ci_high))
cat(sprintf("  First-stage F (HC1)= %.3f\n", fs_F))
```

## 3. Expected Findings
- Sign: Positive. Higher road density should increase accessibility, lower commuting costs, expand labor and product market reach, and make urban areas more attractive, raising population growth.
- Magnitude: Moderate. If variables are approximately standardized (as suggested by the preview range), a 1 SD increase in road density could raise population growth by roughly 0.3–0.7 SD. In levels, this translates to a meaningful but not one-for-one effect. IV estimates should be larger than OLS if roads were targeted to declining areas (attenuating OLS), or smaller than OLS if reverse causality dominated.
- Diagnostics: Expect a strong first-stage (F > 10). Robustness checks (adding nonlinear controls, trimming outliers) should leave the sign positive and the magnitude within a similar range.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Use the 1947 highway plan as an instrument for road density.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Increased road density leads to higher population growth in urban areas.
